title: Willing Hearts Bring Gifts for God's Dwelling
summary: Moses gathers Israel, repeats the Sabbath command, and calls for voluntary offerings and skilled workers to build the tabernacle. Men and women whose hearts are stirred bring gold jewelry, yarn, skins, wood, stones, oil, and spices, and skilled women spin yarn and goat hair. Moses announces that God has called Bezalel and Oholiab, filled them with skill, and given them the ability to teach others.
story: With the covenant renewed in chapter 34, the plans Moses received on the mountain in chapters 25 to 31 can finally be carried out. Chapters 35 to 40 tell how Israel built the tabernacle, and they repeat the earlier instructions closely, now as things done rather than things commanded. The mood has changed completely since chapter 32. Then the people demanded gold from their ears for a god they could see, and Aaron took it. Now they bring their gold freely, as much as their hearts prompt, for the God who has forgiven them. The restored people start where God's instructions ended, with the Sabbath, and then begin the work that will end with God's glory filling the tent in chapter 40.
historical:
Israel is still camped at Sinai, some months into its first year after leaving Egypt. The materials they give are costly and suggest the wealth the Egyptians handed over at the exodus (12:35-36). The blue and purple yarn were colored with dye from murex sea snails harvested along the eastern Mediterranean coast, the famous purple of the Phoenician cities, and were among the most expensive goods of the ancient world. Scarlet came from an insect, and fine linen was an Egyptian specialty. The Hebrew word behind fine leather (verse 7) is uncertain; suggestions include the skin of a sea animal such as the dugong, a kind of goat leather, or a particular color of dyed leather.

Accounts of temple building from elsewhere in the ancient Near East follow a familiar sequence: a divine command and plan, gathering of materials and workers, construction, dedication, and blessing. The inscriptions of Gudea, ruler of Lagash in southern Mesopotamia about 2100 BC, describe him receiving a temple plan from his god in a dream and then building it with great care. Exodus 25 to 40 follows the same broad pattern, with one sharp difference: the builders are not a king's conscripted laborers but a whole people giving and working voluntarily.
cultural:
Voluntary giving is the chapter's theme. Everyone whose heart was willing or stirred brought something, and the text names women explicitly several times (verses 22, 25, 26, 29). Spinning yarn and goat hair was women's skilled work in the ancient household, and the chapter treats it as part of the sacred task alongside metalwork and carving. Black goat-hair cloth is still used for Bedouin tents because it sheds rain and holds warmth, and the tent spread over the tabernacle's inner linen curtains was made from it (26:7). The gold was presented as a wave offering (verse 22), a gesture of lifting or moving a gift before the LORD to dedicate it to him.

Verse 3, forbidding fire in any dwelling on the Sabbath, is not found in the earlier Sabbath law of chapter 31. In the wilderness, lighting a fire meant gathering fuel and doing real work. The verse shaped later Jewish practice. Rabbinic tradition understood it to forbid kindling fire on the Sabbath but not having a fire already lit, so Sabbath lamps and candles are lit before sundown; Karaite Jews historically read it more strictly and kept no fire burning at all.
literary: The chapter opens a long section (35:1 to 40:33) that mirrors chapters 25 to 31. Here the order is changed: the Sabbath, which closed the instructions, now opens the construction. Moses' appeal (verses 4-19) lists the materials and then the finished items in an inventory that condenses the earlier chapters. The response (verses 20-29) is told with a repeated refrain about the heart: willing, stirred, prompted, skilled. The call of Bezalel and Oholiab (verses 30-35) repeats 31:1-6 almost word for word, with one addition: God has given them the ability to teach others (verse 34). The chapter's structure, command followed by exact obedience, is the literary form of a restored relationship.

outline.t: A call for skilled workers and the list of what they will make
Men and women bring their gifts
Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with skill and able to teach

doctrines.note: Moses repeats that God has filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God for artistic and technical work, and verse 34 adds that the Spirit's gift includes the ability to teach others. The Spirit's gifts multiply through the community rather than staying with one gifted person.

The whole congregation, leaders and ordinary people, men and women, builds God's dwelling together. Every gift is different and every one is needed, from gemstones to goat hair. The picture anticipates the New Testament's description of the church as a body in which each part does its work.
The same word for wisdom describes the craftsmen and the women who spin. Skill in ordinary tasks, offered to God, is treated as a form of wisdom he gives.

words.note: Lev, heart, used nine times in this chapter. In Hebrew the heart is the center of will, thought, and desire, not only emotion. Willing hearts bring gifts, and wise hearts do skilled work. The chapter locates the source of both in the inner person.

Nadav, to be willing or to offer freely. From it comes nedavah, the freewill offering (verse 29), a gift beyond what the law required. It stands in deliberate contrast to the demanded gold of the calf.

Terumah, contribution or offering, from a verb meaning to lift up. It is the word used in 25:2 for the offering God asked for, and here the people bring it. The word suggests something lifted out of one's own possessions and set apart for God.

Yarah, to teach or instruct. It shares a root with torah, the word for God's instruction or law. Bezalel and Oholiab are given the ability to teach, so the skill God gives becomes something passed on.

christ: The New Testament speaks of a new dwelling for God built by a willing and gifted people. Jesus spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21), and Paul describes the church as a holy temple being built together into a dwelling for God by his Spirit (Ephesians 2:21-22), with each member given gifts for building up the body (Ephesians 4:11-16). Paul's appeal for the collection for the poor in Jerusalem echoes the freewill spirit of this chapter: each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Luke notes that women supported Jesus and the twelve from their own means (Luke 8:1-3), much as women's skilled work and gifts built the tabernacle. These are thematic parallels rather than predictions.

hard.q: Why does Exodus repeat the tabernacle instructions almost word for word?
hard.a: Modern readers often find chapters 35 to 40 tedious, since so much repeats chapters 25 to 31. Several explanations work together. First, repetition was a normal feature of ancient writing, especially building accounts: command and fulfillment were both recorded to show that the work was done exactly as ordered. Second, the repetition has theological weight after the golden calf. The people who had made an image of their own design now build God's dwelling precisely according to his design, and the text wants the reader to see the match. Third, in an age when texts were read aloud, repetition helped memory and gave a sense of completeness. Critical scholars also note that the Greek Septuagint arranges these closing chapters in a noticeably different order from the Hebrew, which suggests they circulated in more than one form before the text settled. Whatever the history, the final shape makes obedience visible.

questions: The same people who gave their gold for the calf now gave it for the tabernacle. What would it mean to redirect something you have used badly toward God's purposes?
The chapter repeatedly mentions willing and stirred hearts. What stirs your heart to give, and what makes giving feel like compulsion?
Spinning goat hair is listed alongside cutting gemstones. What ordinary skill of yours could serve God and others?
